title: The Planted Answer
blurb: The wrong answers Microsoft planted for Domain 2 — twin scenarios that differ by the exact fact the exam flips.

pairs.dimension: governance container vs the workspace where you build

a.text: The platform team needs one place to manage shared security, connections, compute and quota for all AI teams.
a.why: The hub is the top-level collaboration and governance container with shared resources — histack trap #3.

b.text: A product team needs the place where their deployments, agents, data and evaluations actually live.
b.why: A project lives inside a hub and is where you actually build — deployments, agents, data, evaluations.

pairs.dimension: the name your code calls vs the base model family

a.text: Your code passes 'chat-app-prod' — the custom name chosen at deploy time — as the model argument in chat.completions.create.
a.why: The deployment name — not the base model name — is what your code calls (histack's exact trap; corpus pair #19).

b.text: The Foundry catalog lists gpt-4o with its benchmark scores before anything is deployed.
b.why: gpt-4o is the base model id in the catalog; it becomes callable only through a named deployment.

pairs.dimension: the resource address you connect to vs the secret that authenticates the call

a.text: A developer configures the client with the Foundry resource's HTTPS address, read from an environment variable, so every request knows which resource on Azure to reach.
a.why: The endpoint (azure_endpoint) is the resource address the SDK targets — it identifies where the call is sent, not who is allowed to send it.

b.text: A developer moves a secret out of the source file into a separate environment variable, so the credential that proves the caller's identity is never hard-coded.
b.why: The credential is passed as api_key (os.getenv('AZURE_OPENAI_KEY')) and authenticates the caller — a privacy-and-security habit distinct from routing.

pairs.dimension: a stateful, tool-using resource vs a single stateless completion request

a.text: A Foundry resource is created once with a name, instructions and attached tools, then referenced across many later turns by follow-up requests using the same conversation.
a.why: An agent is a persistent, named resource — created via PromptAgentDefinition with instructions and tools, then invoked repeatedly.

b.text: A script sends messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Summarize this case.'}] and gets one reply back from a plain completions request, with nothing saved on the server and no thread or tools involved.
b.why: A bare chat.completions.create is a single stateless request — no persisted instructions, tools or identity survive between calls.

pairs.dimension: where behavioral rules belong in the message stack

a.text: 'Always return customer details in a fixed JSON shape and only answer HR-policy questions' — a persistent rule for every turn.
a.why: Persona, tone, rules and guardrails belong in the system prompt — histack's 'single most-tested distinction'; the planted wrong answer puts behavior in the user prompt or deployment settings.

b.text: 'Summarize this quarter's absence report for me' — one request, this turn only.
b.why: The user prompt carries this turn's request; prior model replies replayed for memory are assistant messages.

pairs.dimension: testing in the portal with no code vs the programmatic path your app ships with

a.text: After deploying a model, a developer types a prompt directly into the Foundry portal and reads the reply on screen without writing a single line of Python.
a.why: The playground is Foundry's on-demand, no-code environment for rapid prototyping and validation before any production code exists.

b.text: The same developer copies the Code tab's snippet, which constructs an AzureOpenAI client and calls chat.completions.create from a Python file the app will actually run.
b.why: The Code tab hands you the programmatic access pattern — the SDK call is what ships, not the portal session that validated it.

pairs.dimension: the behavioral rules an agent follows vs the capabilities it can invoke

a.text: A prompt agent is configured so it always responds in a formal tone and refuses to discuss competitor pricing, no matter what the user asks.
a.why: Persona and behavioral rules supplied to PromptAgentDefinition are instructions — they shape how the agent responds, not what it can do.

b.text: The same agent is given web search and file search so it can look up live information instead of relying only on what it already knows.
b.why: Web search and file search are attached from the Build > Tools catalog — capabilities the agent can invoke, separate from its instructions.

pairs.dimension: changing model weights vs injecting current data at inference

a.text: The model must always answer in your firm's house style, learned from 5,000 past examples.
a.why: Fine-tuning retrains weights on examples — the tool for durable style/behavior change.

b.text: The model must answer from this month's price list, which changes weekly, without retraining.
b.why: RAG injects retrieved current org data at inference — 'feeding the model your own data so answers stay accurate'.

pairs.dimension: reserved hourly capacity vs pay-per-token elastic pricing

a.text: A batch workload needs a predictable, guaranteed processing rate at a fixed hourly cost, reserved in advance regardless of how many tokens are actually sent.
a.why: PTU reserves dedicated hourly capacity for predictable, high-volume throughput — you pay for the reservation, not per token.

b.text: An interactive chat app has unpredictable traffic and needs pay-per-token billing with regional, data zone, or global processing options, rather than hourly reserved capacity.
b.why: Standard deployment is the preferred option offering the widest range of capabilities and elastic pay-per-token pricing — the exam's most-tested deployment contrast (pair #27).

pairs.dimension: defining the analyzer vs running it

a.text: You have written a custom field schema for supplier contracts and must register it before any document is processed.
a.why: Creating/defining the analyzer from a field schema is setup, not execution.

b.text: The analyzer already exists; the code runs it against a contract URL and polls for the structured result.
b.why: Execution is begin_analyze(analyzer_id=…, inputs=[AnalysisInput(url=…)]) — the close-method-name swap the corpus documents (pair #26).

pairs.dimension: multimodal LLM-reasoned extraction vs deterministic known-form extraction

a.text: Describe the fields you want in natural language and extract them from a mix of PDFs, images and meeting audio into structured JSON.
a.why: CU lets you describe fields in natural language while an LLM reasons over multimodal input — histack's cue: 'free-form or non-document input'.

b.text: Extract totals from a high volume of standard invoices and receipts using a ready-made model.
b.why: Deterministic extraction from known form types — invoices, receipts, IDs, business cards. 'The extraction trap', histack's favorite.

pairs.dimension: pulling structured fields out of raw content vs indexing content for later retrieval

a.text: A retail team sends shelf photos in and gets back structured product fields such as name, price and quantity, defined by their own schema.
a.why: Content Understanding turns raw, unstructured or multimodal input into the specific structured output a schema asks for.

b.text: A RAG chatbot needs a knowledge base it can query by semantic similarity so a chat model can ground its answers in the retrieved passages.
b.why: Azure AI Search indexes content — often via embeddings — and retrieves it at query time; RAG patterns pair a chat model with AI Search for grounding, a different job from extracting fields from a document.
